one_liner: Fully unrolled Go LEB128/protobuf varint decoder, roughly 1.3x-2.9x faster per call than encoding/binary.Uvarint on Go 1.17.3.
what_it_does: Decodes unsigned LEB128 (protobuf) varints from a byte slice with the same signature and error convention as binary.Uvarint: (value, n) where n == 0 means the buffer is too short and n < 0 means overflow. It also offers UvarintSize (encoded length of a uint64, like gogo/protobuf's sov helpers) and ProtoTag, which decodes and validates a protobuf field-number/wire-type key in one pass. There is no encoder (use binary.PutUvarint) and no signed or zigzag Varint.
how_it_is_fast: The decode loop is fully unrolled into ten byte steps, each with an early return. When the input slice is at least 10 bytes long, one up-front length test lets the Go compiler drop the per-byte bounds checks. Shorter slices take a second unrolled path that checks the length at each step. UvarintSize replaces the shift-and-count loop with a small binary tree of comparisons against precomputed MaxValN constants.
when_to_use: Go code that decodes many individual varints in a hand-written protobuf, LEB128 or log-format parser, where binary.Uvarint shows up in profiles.
Buffers that usually have 10 or more bytes left past the varint (streams, large messages), which hit the bounds-check-free path; the README's _large rows show the biggest gains there.
Size precomputation before encoding (UvarintSize), e.g. to size a buffer exactly before marshalling.
Protobuf key parsing where you want field number and wire type validated in the same pass (ProtoTag).
when_not_to_use: Bulk integer arrays where you control the format: block codecs (Stream VByte, SIMD bit packing, FastPFor) decode orders of magnitude more integers per second than any per-value LEB128 decoder.
C++ projects: this is Go only, and the catalog's C++/Rust siblings (varint-simd, MaskedVByte, Stream VByte) are the relevant options.
When you also need a faster encoder or signed/zigzag varints; the package only decodes unsigned values and computes sizes.
If you need speedup figures for a current Go toolchain: the README table was produced with Go 1.17.3 (2021), CI still pins Go 1.17.x, and nobody has re-measured on newer compilers.

integration.platforms: any Go target; pure Go, no assembly; a 2021 commit fixed protobuf tag decoding on 32-bit architectures
integration.thread_safety: Stateless pure functions; safe for concurrent use (not stated in docs, follows from the code).
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: Uvarint has the same signature and the same return values as binary.Uvarint, including -11 for reads past 10 bytes (tests compare both on short, overflow and long buffers), but there is no PutUvarint, Varint, ReadUvarint or io.ByteReader variant.

gotchas: Before commit 44109b0 (2021-11-16) an overflowing input made Uvarint scan the rest of the buffer and return -(11+j); it now stops at 10 bytes and returns -11, matching Go 1.17's fix for golang/go#41185. Pin a version from November 2021 or later.

ProtoTag decodes at most 9 bytes and returns an int64 field number without checking protobuf's 2^29-1 limit. It rejects field 0 only in the 1-byte form, so an overlong encoding such as 0x81 0x00 returns num 0 with n 2. Callers still need a range check.
The README calls this an encoding/decoding package, but the only encoder-side helper is UvarintSize.

The benchmarks decode a single constant value in a loop, so branch prediction is perfect. The UvarintSize 'old' column has no stdlib counterpart (encoding/binary has no size function); the test file's loop version (uvarintSizeLoop) appears to be what it measured.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over chmike/varint when you only need a drop-in faster binary.Uvarint with identical error semantics plus a protobuf tag helper; chmike/varint covers encoding as well and publishes a dated i5-11400 table. Pick streamvbyte-simdgo instead when you can change the wire format to a block codec and want throughput rather than per-value latency.
verified_claims_summary: The README benchcmp table compares this package's Uvarint against binary.Uvarint for 1-9-byte values decoded repeatedly from 'exact' and 16-byte buffers. Per call it drops from 3.46 to 2.64 ns (1 byte) and from 14.1 to 4.89 ns (8 bytes, large buffer). UvarintSize runs in 0.43-1.00 ns versus 1.71-6.64 ns for a loop. Per the 2021-11-19 commit the numbers come from Go 1.17.3 with GOMAXPROCS 8; CPU model not stated.
status_note: Small (about 200 lines of decode logic), MIT-licensed and easy to vendor; untouched from 2021 until a 2026-05-01 commit that only adds tests, so treat it as finished rather than actively developed.
